sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Independently re-read the complete original MCP unit. The dynamic refresh section requires explicit refresh() and says a call before refresh_interval elapses since the previous check returns immediately. It also assigns sentinel changes to ordinary-setting reloads. The v3 schedule makes every possible preceding ordinary check at least 119 seconds before a later invocation, eliminating the former 45-versus-60-second early-return ambiguity without inventing SDK ordering. Production provider configuration guidance supports these scoped baseline mechanics, not an all-features release assertion.

Independently re-read the complete original MCP reference unit. It documents versionless references, keyvault_credential and separate resource access, then explicitly describes secret_refresh_interval in seconds and retrieval during refresh() after that interval even without changes in the App Configuration store. A successful initial retrieval and successful bounded later calls are scenario premises, not Azure latency promises. Those rules support B and contradict sentinel-only C; no blanket HSM protection, automatic arbitrary-secret rotation policy or unconditional refresh claim from the broader article is adopted.

choiceReviews.rationale: At t=240, the secret age is still 240 seconds from its last retrieval at t=0, below the documented 300-second secret interval. The ordinary gate is clear because the preceding call completed by t=121, but clearing that separate 60-second gate does not make the secret interval due. This time could qualify with a shorter secret interval, not the specified one.

The first listed invocation after the secret interval is t=360; calls at t=120 and t=240 occur before 300 seconds. The previous ordinary check must have completed by t=241, so even the shortest possible gap at t=360 is 119 seconds, greater than 60. Both gates are therefore clear regardless of their internal check order. The reference unit permits independent secret refresh despite an unchanged sentinel, and the question asks timing eligibility rather than an unconditional delivery guarantee.

A changed watched sentinel signals ordinary-setting reloads in the connection unit. The reference unit separately says secret_refresh_interval can retrieve updated Key Vault values even when the App Configuration reference/store does not change. Requiring a sentinel change would be appropriate for the ordinary-setting path, but it is not a necessary precondition for this independently configured secret refresh.

That changed interval is a counterexample setting, not a claim that the supplied 300 behaves differently.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The original reference unit defines secret_refresh_interval in seconds and retrieves fresh secrets when that independent interval has elapsed during refresh(). The connection unit separately gates ordinary checks by refresh_interval. Their separation prevents an ordinary-eligible t=240 call from satisfying the unchanged 300-second secret interval.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The t=360 invocation is the first listed call whose timing permits the independently configured secret refresh.

At t=360 the secret interval is elapsed, and the preceding ordinary check cannot be later than t=241, leaving at least 119 seconds against its 60-second gate. Testing either interval first therefore leaves the timing eligible; no internal SDK ordering assertion is needed.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: This answer fits the supplied versionless-reference schedule, explicit t=0 completion origins and successful bounded calls, with a replacement version available before the first secret-due invocation. optionChallenges.claimRepresented: No listed invocation can permit secret re-resolution until the sentinel changes.

That is a different target than the independently aged Key Vault secret in this question; changing the sentinel alone still is not an autonomous scheduler.
